title: She Took a Train From Kalyan to Andheri for Years. Now Sushmita Siingh Walked Cannes and Signed Her First Hollywood-Adjacent Film.
excerpt: The 25-year-old's debut feature Bombay Stories — a Manto-inspired drama co-starring Mouni Roy — premiered on the Croisette, won Best Feature in Paris, and quietly landed her a French production. A genuine outsider's fairy tale, told without the gloss.
body:
Every Cannes produces a thousand photographs and exactly one or two real stories. This year, one of them belongs to a girl who used to ride the Mumbai local from **Kalyan to Andheri** every single day, chasing auditions that mostly ended in rejection.

Her name is **Sushmita Siingh**, she is 25, and her debut feature **Bombay Stories** didn't just get her a red-carpet selfie at the 79th Cannes Film Festival — it walked her straight into the kind of career turn that Bollywood's star kids are handed at birth and outsiders spend a decade praying for. Directed by **Rahhat Shah Kazmi** and inspired by the searing short fiction of **Saadat Hasan Manto**, the film premiered on the Croisette last month, was selected in the Asian Panorama section at the Da Nang Asian Film Festival, and took home **Best Feature Film at the Paris Film Awards**. Not bad for a first outing.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=gf1OVw-zUxM</youtube>


> "You dream of moments like these, but you never imagine your debut film itself will take you to the world's biggest film festival. I remember every audition, every rejection, every train ride, every sacrifice — and suddenly all of it felt worth it." — Sushmita Siingh

In *Bombay Stories*, Siingh plays a 20-year-old college student whose life detonates after a traumatic incident — a role rooted in prostitution and trauma, the kind of part that either makes a young actor or swallows her whole. She shares the frame with **Mouni Roy** and **Anupriya Goenka**, and to hear her tell it, the hardest part wasn't the cameras. It was the carrying.

"Since the film touches on prostitution and trauma, I had to enter a very dark, vulnerable emotional space," she told *Filmfare*. "There were days when I would carry the character home with me because the emotions felt so real. It transformed me as an actor." Manto, who spent his career writing the women polite society pretended not to see, would have recognised the cost.

The glamour, when it came, came humbled. Working opposite Mouni Roy — a bona fide screen star with a fan base that spans continents — could have intimidated a newcomer. Instead, Siingh walked away talking about humility. "Beyond their success and fame, what stood out most was their kindness. It reminded me that no matter how big you become, your humanity is what truly defines you." It is the sort of thing every debutante says, except she says it like she means it, because she has watched the other version up close on a hundred audition floors.

And here is where the fairy tale stops being a metaphor. Somewhere between the screenings and the red carpets at Cannes, Siingh found herself in conversation with the team of French filmmaker **Eric Atlan** and producer **Rex Christy**. There were other actors already in the running. She auditioned anyway. She got the part.

"I had gone to Cannes because of *Bombay Stories*, and somewhere amidst all the screenings and conversations, I ended up meeting the team," she said. "After the audition process, I somehow found myself being chosen for the role. This project marks my first international film. Firsts are always unforgettable." She has signed it. A girl from Kalyan, in a French production, because she happened to show up to her own premiere and refused to be just a tourist on the carpet.

That clarity about what Cannes is *for* runs through everything she says. Asked about the annual online grumbling that the festival has become a circus of brands and influencers, Siingh pushed back with the quiet conviction of someone who earned her invitation. "Somewhere the essence is getting misunderstood online. Cannes is, first and foremost, a film festival — a celebration of cinema and artists from around the world. There's nothing wrong with brands or fashion being present, but people should remember the soul of Cannes has always been cinema." Coming from the only person on this list who actually had a *film* in competition, it lands harder than any couture gown.

Her origin story is almost suspiciously cinematic. A self-described tomboy told she could never model, she became, at 17, the **first Indian and Asian to win Miss Teen World 2019** — a title that cracked the door open. It was her mother, she says, who saw it first. "It was my mother who saw something in me before I saw it in myself."

For the diaspora, Siingh's rise is the kind of story that travels well — proof that the pipeline from a Mumbai suburb to the French Riviera is real, if brutally narrow. *Bombay Stories*, with its festival pedigree and Manto bones, is exactly the sort of Indian arthouse film that finds its diaspora audience through festival circuits, curated streaming platforms and word of mouth rather than a Friday multiplex blitz; keep an eye on regional film festivals across the **US, UK and Canada**, where titles like this tend to surface for one glorious weekend before vanishing.

The star kids will have their summer of trailers and box-office wars. But the most quietly thrilling Indian story of this Cannes belongs to the girl who took the train.
